title: Adaptive window batcher for streaming chat: KV-aware grouping and GPU memory caps
creator: Alicia Park
description:
Problem: Our current continuous batching for streaming chat groups requests purely by time-window and sequence length heuristics. This causes GPU memory spikes when multiple long-context streams with large KV caches arrive concurrently and degrades latency SLOs for short-lived interactive sessions. Goal: Implement an adaptive window batcher that is KV-aware, enforces per-GPU memory caps, and biases formation for low-latency interactive streams while preserving throughput for background/throughput workloads. The batcher must support streaming token-by-token output (server-side streaming) without blocking generation for already-started streams.

Scope: PoC runtime change + canary rollout on a subset of Dedicated pools. Deliverables: design doc, implementation in runtime batcher, unit/integration tests, perf benchmark, console metric dashboards, rollout runbook with rollback criteria.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New batcher groups streaming chat requests such that 95th percentile GPU memory utilization per device reduces by >=12% under synthetic multi-long-context traffic; 2) Median latency for short interactive sessions (<128 tokens) does not increase more than 10ms; 3) No increase in token-level error (decoding anomalies) across canary traffic; 4) Feature toggle present with three modes: off, conservative, aggressive; 5) Metrics emitted: batch_size_distribution, per_batch_kv_bytes, per_gpu_mem_reserved, preemption_events; 6) End-to-end integration test that simulates 500 concurrent streams with mixed contexts passes within SLOs.
notes: Initial investigation identified two root causes: unbounded KV cache accumulation across co-located streams and naive time-window that over-batches long contexts.
We will maintain streaming semantics: once a stream starts generating, subsequent token sends for that stream must be routable to the same KV cache slot until completion or explicit eviction.
Memory estimator: per-request estimated_kv_bytes computed from context_length * kv_bytes_per_token (profiled per-model/quantization). We'll calibrate per-model constants from runtime sampling.
Adaptive window logic: dynamic_timer = base_timer * (1 + alpha * median_recent_kv_bytes_normalized). Conservative mode uses alpha=2.0, aggressive uses alpha=0.25.
Batch formation policy: sort pending streams by priority_score = latency_weight * inverse_client_ttl + size_weight * estimated_kv_bytes. Priority weights are configurable per route.

Preemption: If adding a request would exceed per-GPU reserved mem cap, try cross-device placement (if same model exists). If no capacity, either flush current batch or defer low-priority streams and emit a preemption_event metric.

KV slot lifecycle: Use LRU with pinning for active streaming sessions. When memory pressure is high, evict cold KV slots before deferring new requests. Evictions must log reason and affected session ids (anonymized) for postmortem.
Compatibility: Must interoperate with existing fallback routing (model-variant fallback) and with console rollouts (canary config).
implementation_steps: 1) Add per-request estimated_kv_bytes field to the incoming request envelope and update SDK wrappers (backwards compatible fallback if missing).
2) Implement GPU memory reservation bookkeeping in dispatcher to track reserved_by_batch and reserved_by_kv_slots, include soft/hard caps per device.
3) Implement adaptive window timer and priority queue for pending streaming start events (C++ runtime).
4) Integrate KV-aware bin-packing when forming batches: choose subset of pending streams with total_estimated_kv + current_batch_kv <= device_soft_cap.
5) Add preemption and defer logic with metrics and audit log entries.
6) Add end-to-end integration test harness that mirrors live traffic shapes and verifies memory and latency targets.
7) Create PRs and link to infra canary configs, update deployment manifests and console feature toggle.
tradeoffs_and_decisions: Decision: Use estimate-based admission rather than exact pre-allocation. Exact pre-allocation would require materializing KV in GPU memory before batching which adds more latency and complexity.

Tradeoff: Conservative mode favors latency at cost of throughput. Aggressive mode favors throughput but increases risk of memory related preemptions. We'll default to conservative for hosted API and allow aggressive for Dedicated reserved pools.

Decision: Keep KV slots tied to session affinity (same device) to avoid expensive KV transfer between GPUs. Cross-device placement only attempted when models are identical and transfer cost predicted to be <= 20ms.
Tradeoff: Per-request estimate errors may cause occasional overcommit; mitigate by exponential backoff on retries and fast evict path for cold sessions.
tests_and_benchmarks: Unit tests for estimator calibration and priority queue behavior.
Integration test simulating mixed workload: 60% short chat (<128 tokens), 30% medium (128-1024), 10% long (>1024) across 500 concurrent streams.
Perf benchmark: compare baseline vs adaptive batcher under synthetic spike (burst of 200 long-context streams) and steady-state load.
Failure mode tests: simulate mis-estimated kv_bytes and ensure preemption metrics fire and system recovers without token corruption.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag; unit/integration tests green. 2) Canary on 5% of Dedicated pool (non-prod first) for 48h, monitor batcher metrics and GPU mem usage. 3) Expand canary to 20% if stable for 72h. 4) Opt-in Dedicated customers with low-latency SLAs enable conservative mode. 5) Full rollout after 2 weeks with monitoring and a 1-hour rollback window. Rollback criteria: >3% increase in token error rate, >10% increase in short-session median latency, or sustained GPU OOMs in canary pool.
